title: The 37% rule
hook: Picking the best of options you can't go back to? Pass on the first 37%.
peek: Suppose you must choose the best of many options, seen one at a time, with no going back. Mathematics gives a clear rule: let the first 37% pass, then take the first one better than all of them. It wins about 37% of the time.
lede: Mathematicians call it the secretary problem. Candidates arrive one by one in random order, and after each you must hire or reject on the spot. You only win if you pick the very best. The optimal plan is to watch the first 37% without choosing, then take the next one who beats them all. The success rate is also about 37%.

bullets.text: The number is 1 divided by e, about 0.368, where e is the constant 2.718 that also turns up in compound interest. For a small field of 10 candidates, the best plan is to let the first three go by.

The surprise is that the chance of success does not keep falling as the field grows. With a hundred candidates or a million, the rule still lands the very best about 37% of the time, far better than a random pick.

The puzzle spread widely after Martin Gardner described it in Scientific American in 1960 as the game of googol. Slips of paper with hidden numbers are turned over one at a time, and you must stop at the largest.
The rule assumes you know how many options there are, can rank them and care only about the very best. If the best happens to sit in the first 37%, you pass it by and end up with the last option.
